question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

1.text:
In CFOP the U–layer is already an oriented U. Up to a vertical rotation
the oriented U–layer is the set

* 4 U–edges  $U_{F},U_{R},U_{B},U_{L}$,
* 4 U–corners $U_{FR},U_{RL},U_{BL},U_{LF}$,

of which the up–sticker is by construction the U colour.  Hence after OLL
a piece of the U–slice is distinguished on the U–layer by the colour
that it shows on the side faces.  An U–edge is distinguished by the one
side sticker that it shows on the four side centres and a U–corner is
distinguished by either of its two side stickers.  Up to a rotation about
the U axis the permutation of the four edges and the permutation of the
four corners is the whole PLL information.  In particular a piece by
piece identification of the U–slice needs one distinguishing side
sticker per piece, i.e. four edge side stickers and four corner side
stickers,

$4_{e}+4_{c}=8$

distinguishing non–U stickers in total.  The U–slice carries

$4\times2\;{\rm corner\;side\;stickers}+4\times1\;{\rm edge\;side\;
stickers}=12$

non–U stickers, eight of which are sufficient for a piece–by–piece
identification and, up to the obvious parity of the U–slice, seven of
which are already information–theoretically enough.  In the usual
front/right view this is the six distinct U–slice side stickers that are
simultaneously visible, three on the front U row and three on the right
U row, the twelve stickers of the whole U slice being the information
that has to be inspectable.  This is the eight sticker, i.e. the twelve
non–up sticker, description of the U slice that is normally quoted as
the PLL recognition information.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented by OLL so that the 8 U stickers

* 4 U edges
* 4 U corners

are all the same colour.  The U face therefore carries no permutation
information at all.  The permutation information of the last layer is
carried entirely by the side stickers that belong to the U layer.

On the U layer

* each U edge contributes one side sticker,
* each U corner contributes two side stickers,

so that the U layer has

4×1 + 4×2 = 12

non-U stickers, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side stickers.
It is that 12 sticker set that carries the whole U permutation.

In terms of distinct pieces the information can be quoted per piece.
An edge is identified by its single side colour and a corner is
identified, its U sticker being U, by a single side colour, so one side
sticker per piece is enough to name the piece.  Hence one side sticker
for each of the 4 U edges and one side sticker for each of the 4 U
corners, i.e. 8 distinct non-U stickers, is an informationally complete
set for the U permutation.  By the usual parity constraint of a
cube the eight pieces are not independent, so in principle 7 distinct
non-U stickers are enough to determine the eighth piece and therefore
the PLL case.  This is the 4×1 + 4×2 = 12 sticker U–layer side set
that is normally quoted as the “U–layer side information’’ for PLL.

2.text:
In the CFOP model the whole of the last step is the permutation of the four
U-slice pieces.  After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the U face itself
gives you no information at all.  The information that is left in the
U–slice is the side information of the four U–corners and the four U–
edges.

* a U–corner has two stickers which are not on U;
* a U–edge has one sticker which is not on U.

Hence on the U–slice there are

4 corners × 2 side–stickers = 8
4 edges × 1 side–sticker  = 4

12 non–U stickers in all, 8 of them belonging to the four U corners and
4 of them belonging to the four U edges.  It is those 12 side stickers
which code the 4!×4!  = 576 permutations of the last layer and, after the
usual rotation equivalence, the 21 PLL algorithms you meet in practice.
That is the information that has to be read.

In practice you do not have to read all 12 of them.  Because the cube
has to be a legal cube the corner parity is the edge parity and the
four pieces are distinguishable up to rotation.  Information theoretically
the 72 rotation–distinct PLL permutations can be distinguished with
≈log6 72 ≈ 2.3 stickers and in real life a cuber recognises a case
from the side colour of the four U edges together with the side colour
of two, and in the worst case four, U corners.  The usual teaching
form is to quote the 8 corner–side stickers – i.e. four corners with the
two visible side stickers each – and the four edge side stickers, the
whole 12 sticker U–slice.  This is the 8+4 =12 non–U stickers that are
in principle available and which in the worst case have to be inspected
to name the case uniquely; the usual working minimum quoted in the
literature is 7–8 distinct side stickers, essentially the four edge
side stickers plus the side information of the four corners.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the U stickers carry no permutation information. The PLL is a permutation of the 4 U edges and 4 U corners. 

Each U edge has exactly one non-U sticker and that sticker is the only way to tell which edge piece is in that U slot. That is 4 stickers.

Each U corner has two non-U stickers. In practice you need at least one distinguishable side sticker per corner to know which corner piece is sitting in the U slot and how it is oriented relative to the other corners. That is 4 further stickers.

With one side sticker per edge and one side sticker per corner you can read the whole U-layer permutation, so 4 + 4 = 8 non-top-facing stickers are required in the worst case to unambiguously identify the PLL case. Fewer than that leaves at least two distinct PLL cases indistinguishable from the information you can see.

5.text:
In an OLL-solved position the U-face is monochrome so the only
information that can separate the 8 U-slice cubies is the colour that
they show on their lateral faces.

On the U-slice

* 4 U-edges : each U-edge has the U-colour on top and one lateral
colour on the side.  4 lateral edge stickers
* 4 U-corners : each U-corner has the U-colour on top and two lateral
colours, one on each of the two side faces that meet at the corner.
4 × 2 = 8 lateral corner stickers

That is

4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12

non-U stickers belonging to the last layer.  In the absolute sense
the state of the U-slice, and hence the exact permutation class of
the last layer, is the arrangement of those 12 lateral stickers.  Up
to a vertical rotation it is the 12-sticker pattern of the U-slice
that is the PLL.

In practice the pattern is highly redundant and a human recogniser
gets away with a great deal less.  The four U-edge side colours
already determine the EPLL part of the case and a single lateral
colour from each of the four U-corners is enough to fix the corner
permutation up to the vertical symmetry of the cube, i.e. the
recognition that is normally taught is done on the 4 + 4 = 8
distinct lateral stickers that are visible on the four U-cubies.  The
12 stickers are the complete, non-redundant, information content of
the last layer.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is a solid colour, so the U stickers themselves give no distinguishing information. Identity of a U-layer piece has to come from its side stickers. There are eight U-layer pieces, four edges and four corners, and each piece is uniquely identified by at least one visible side sticker once the top is oriented. In practice you can recognise a PLL by checking the four U-edge side colours and the four U-corner side colours, i.e. one identifying sticker per piece. That is eight non-U stickers, four edge stickers and four corner stickers, which is the amount of side information that is normally inspected for a complete, unambiguous PLL identification.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP PLL recognition problem after OLL. U face is monochrome, so no permutation information is on the U stickers themselves. Information is in the side stickers of the U-slice.

U-slice composition:
* 4 U-edges: each has 1 non-U side sticker → 4 edge side stickers
* 4 U-corners: each has 2 non-U side stickers → 8 corner side stickers
Total non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 4 + 8 = 12.

All colleagues agree on the 12-sticker inventory. Disagreement is about how many must be *seen* to unambiguously name a PLL case.

Piece-by-piece identification argument: an edge is identified by its single side colour; a corner is identified up to U-orientation by at least one of its two side colours. Hence one distinguishing side sticker per piece is information-theoretically sufficient: 4 edges + 4 corners = 8 distinct non-U stickers. This is the 4+4 =8 figure quoted by Colleagues 1,4,6 and the “usual working minimum” in Colleagues 2,3,5.

Redundancy / parity: the U-slice is not independent, corner parity = edge parity, so the eighth piece is determined by the other seven. Hence an information-theoretic lower bound of ~7 distinct non-U stickers is often noted, and ≈log6 72 ≈2.3 stickers in an ideal coding sense. Colleagues 1-3 note this.

Practical recognition: in a fixed front/right view only 6 distinct U-slice side stickers are simultaneously visible – 3 on the front U row and 3 on the right U row. The complete 12-sticker pattern is the full, non-redundant description of the U permutation; the 8-sticker, one-per-piece set is the normally taught sufficient set.

Current belief: the complete U-layer side information is 12 non-U stickers; 8 non-U stickers, i.e. one identifying sticker per U piece, 4 edge side +4 corner side, is sufficient for unambiguous PLL identification in the worst case, with 7 being the parity-reduced theoretical minimum. Unresolved: whether the question asks for the total inventory 12 or the minimal sufficient 8. Consensus in the room leans to 8 as the practical “must be seen” number.
